(1) Which name matches CH3CH2CH2COOH?
A. Butanoic acid
B. Propanoic acid
C. Butan-1-ol
D. Ethyl ethanoate [1]

(2) Why does fractional distillation separate petroleum fractions?

B. They have different boiling ranges
C. They have different solubilities in water

B. Kerosene
C. Naphtha
D. Refinery gas [1]

A. They contain equal numbers of carbons
B. They have the same molecular formula
C. They have the same boiling point
D. They contain the same functional group [1]

(5) Why can restricting a methane burner’s air supply lead to carbon monoxide?
A. Extra oxygen causes incomplete combustion
B. Restricted air permits complete carbon oxidation
C. Restricted air guarantees carbon dioxide only
D. Less oxygen permits incomplete combustion [1]

(6) Which statement distinguishes cracking from fractional distillation?
A. Cracking condenses vapour without chemical change
B. Cracking separates unchanged molecules by boiling range
C. Cracking breaks larger molecules into smaller ones
D. Cracking joins small molecules into longer chains [1]

(7) Which pair forms during complete combustion of ethanol?
A. Carbon monoxide and carbon
B. Ethene and hydrogen
C. Carbon dioxide and water
D. Ethanoic acid and hydrogen [1]

(8) Which account describes formation of ethyl ethanoate?
A. Alcohol + acid → ester + water
B. Alcohol + acid → ester + hydrogen
C. Alcohol + alkali → ester + water
D. Alkene + steam → ester only [1]

(9) Which monomer matches [–CH2–CHCl–]n?
A. CH3CH2Cl
B. CH2ClCH2Cl
C. CH2=CHCl
D. CHCl=CHCl [1]

(10) Why is an electrically insulating plastic useful as a wire covering?
A. It makes the metal core less conductive
B. It restricts unwanted current paths from the metal
C. It carries current instead of the metal core
D. It prevents heating by absorbing all electrical energy [1]

(11) Which change describes protein hydrolysis?
A. Water joins sugars into longer starch chains
B. Protein chains lengthen without reacting with water
C. Amide links form as water molecules leave
D. Water breaks amide links to release amino acids [1]

(12) Why should hydrolysate and reference spots be developed in the same chromatography run?
A. Matching conditions permit meaningful reference comparisons
B. Matching conditions force all spots together
C. Different solvents improve comparisons of Rf
D. Reference spots belong above the front [1]
items.canonical_answer:
(1) A. Butanoic acid The carboxyl carbon belongs to the four-carbon chain.
Distractor explanations: B: The chain has four carbons including the carboxyl carbon, not three. C: COOH is a carboxylic-acid group, not an alcohol group. D: The structure is an acid, not an ester.

(2) B. They have different boiling ranges. Different volatility allows condensation at different column heights.
Distractor explanations: A: Distillation separates by volatility rather than reaction rate or reactivity. C: The process does not separate fractions by dissolving them in water. D: The separation uses boiling/condensation, not solid melting points.

(3) B. Kerosene Kerosene is the relevant aircraft fuel fraction.
Distractor explanations: A: Bitumen is the heavy road/roofing residue. C: Naphtha is mainly a chemical feedstock in this syllabus. D: Refinery gas is associated with cooking/heating rather than the stated jet fuel.

(4) D. They contain the same functional group. The common functional group governs similar chemistry.
Distractor explanations: A: Successive members differ in carbon count. B: Members have a common general formula but different molecular formulae. C: Boiling points change with chain length.

(5) D. Less oxygen permits incomplete combustion. Incomplete oxidation occurs when oxygen supply is insufficient.
Distractor explanations: A: Insufficient, not extra, oxygen favours incomplete combustion. B: Restricted oxygen can prevent complete oxidation. C: Restricted air can produce CO and soot, so CO2 alone is not guaranteed.

(6) C. Cracking breaks larger molecules into smaller ones Cracking is a chemical conversion, whereas distillation is physical separation.
Distractor explanations: A: Condensation is physical and does not split molecules. B: This describes fractional distillation rather than cracking. D: Joining small units describes polymerisation, not cracking.

(7) C. Carbon dioxide and water Complete oxidation gives CO2 and H2O.
Distractor explanations: A: These are incomplete-combustion carbon products. B: These are not the complete-combustion products. D: Complete combustion goes to carbon dioxide and water, not this acid/hydrogen pair.

(8) A. Alcohol + acid → ester + water An alcohol and carboxylic acid form an ester plus water.
Distractor explanations: B: Esterification produces water, not hydrogen gas. C: The required reactant is a carboxylic acid, not an alkali. D: Alkene hydration produces an alcohol, not an ester.

(9) C. CH2=CHCl Restoring C=C between backbone carbons retains one chlorine substituent.
Distractor explanations: A: This saturated molecule lacks the double bond needed for addition polymerisation. B: It is saturated and has two chlorine atoms per two carbons. D: It has two chlorines per repeat unit rather than one.

(10) B. It restricts unwanted current paths from the metal The coating separates people and other conductors from the conducting metal.
Distractor explanations: A: The coating does not need to reduce the metal’s conductivity. C: The metal core carries current; the covering insulates. D: Insulation does not absorb all energy or guarantee no heating.

Distractor explanations: A: This describes carbohydrate formation, not protein hydrolysis. B: Hydrolysis breaks chains rather than lengthening them. C: Forming amide links and eliminating water is the reverse of hydrolysis.

Distractor explanations: B: Common conditions do not force chemically different spots to coincide. C: Changing solvents changes Rf and makes direct comparison unreliable. D: Reference samples start at the baseline, not above the solvent front.

items.prompt:
(a) Plan chromatography to compare the components of a teacher-prepared carbohydrate hydrolysate with glucose and reference sugar B. Include preparation, apparatus, development, observation and a defensible conclusion. No specific locating-agent identity is required. [6]

(b) State the distances travelled by the lower sample spot and the solvent front from the pencil baseline in the learner panel of ![Learner stimulus](visuals/VIS-6117-10-04-learner.svg). Read the ruler, whose marks are heights above the paper bottom. [2]

(c) Calculate Rf for the lower sample spot using your measurements in part (b). Show your working. [2]

(d) Explain why a wide, wet starting spot can make the chromatogram hard to interpret, and how the spotting procedure should be improved. [2]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Filter a suitable diluted portion of the teacher-prepared hydrolysate if suspended solids remain. Draw a pencil baseline above a shallow solvent reservoir in a covered chamber. Apply small hydrolysate, glucose and B spots in separate lanes, drying between applications. Develop all lanes on the same paper in the same solvent, with the paper upright and solvent initially below the baseline. Remove the paper before the front reaches the top, mark the solvent front immediately, and visualise the spots by a suitable supervised method. Compare positions or Rf values with references: in the chromatography example the two detected sample spots match glucose and B, supporting their possible presence rather than proving unique identities.

(b) Lower sample spot: 2.4 cm from baseline. Solvent front: 8.0 cm from baseline. Subtract the baseline height, 1.0 cm, from the ruler heights 3.4 and 9.0 cm.

(c) Rf = spot distance/front distance = 2.4/8.0 = 0.30, without a unit.

(d) A large wet spot spreads and can make neighbouring component spots overlap. Apply smaller spots with a capillary and dry each application before adding more, so starting spots remain compact.

Part a: Pencil baseline above solvent with suitable chamber/paper arrangement (1).
Part a: Small dried sample and reference spots in separate lanes (1).
Part a: Develop together in covered chamber under the same solvent conditions (1).
Part a: Mark front promptly and visualise spots suitably (1).
Part a: Compare reference positions/Rf for a qualified conclusion (1). Accept equivalent sound sequencing; no named locating chemical required.
Part b: 2.4 cm ±0.1 cm from the baseline (1).
Part b: 8.0 cm ±0.1 cm from the baseline (1). Reject uncorrected heights from paper bottom.
Part c: Divide the candidate’s baseline-to-spot distance by their baseline-to-front distance (1).
Part c: 0.30 with no unit for correct readings; allow correct follow-through from part (b) (1).
Part d: Broad/wet spots spread or overlap, obscuring components (1).
Part d: Smaller applications dried between additions (1).
